title: Am I Being Picky, Or Do I Just Know What I’m Not Doing Again?
summary: Muslim women are often called too picky about marriage. But standards for character, deen, & respect aren’t the same as expecting perfection.
body_markdown:
There’s a pattern I’ve noticed enough times now that I don’t think it’s a coincidence anymore: my family can produce a man’s entire clan history in under five minutes — his lineage, his father’s lineage, which part of the diaspora his people scattered to, whether there’s any old history between our families going back decades. That information moves fast. Nobody has to chase it down.


But the moment I try to explain why something about a man’s character gave me pause — the way he talks about women, the way he goes cold instead of talking things through, the way “practicing” seems to come with rules for me and none for him — the reaction changes completely. Suddenly I’m overthinking it. Suddenly I’m being difficult. Suddenly it’s *no one is perfect, and you’re not getting any younger.*


I’m twenty-five. I want to talk about that gap, because it’s been sitting with me for a while: we will investigate a man’s clan before anyone even considers dinner, but ask me to defend, in detail, why his conduct actually mattered. Somehow the lineage carries more weight than the person. Somehow that’s normal, and I’m the one being unreasonable.


Here’s what nobody prepares you for, growing up in this community: the pressure rarely comes from strangers. It comes from people who love you, who survived things you didn’t have to survive, who left everything so you could have choices — and who are now, in their own way, terrified you’ll waste those choices being “too selective.” I understand, on some level, why “just give him a chance” sounds to them like wisdom instead of what it sometimes actually is, which is fear wearing wisdom’s clothes.


And for a long time I absorbed that fear like it was fact. I’d know, clearly, that something about a person was off, and then I’d spend days arguing myself out of my own read. Maybe I *am* too picky. Maybe I’ve absorbed too much online discourse and started expecting a man who doesn’t exist. Maybe every other woman I know built a life with less than what I’m holding out for, and my standards are just vanity dressed up as self-respect.


Then I’d sit with it a little longer, past the noise, and land in the same place every time: I never wanted anything extravagant. I wanted someone whose deen showed up in how he treated people when nothing was being watched. I wanted to not owe an explanation for wanting a career. I wanted a man who could handle disagreement without going cold and silent for a week, punishing me with distance instead of talking to me. That was the whole list. Other people just kept translating it into “picky” because agreeable was the version of me they were used to.


There’s a word we use — *ceeb* — shame, disgrace, the thing you avoid at all costs because it doesn’t just land on you, it lands on your whole family’s name in a community where everyone already knows everyone’s business. So much of what gets called pickiness is really just a woman refusing to let ceeb-avoidance make her decisions for her. Saying no to a bad match feels riskier than the match itself, because a no gets talked about. A yes, even a bad one, gets quietly absorbed into “she’s married, alhamdulillah,” and nobody asks any more questions after that.


I think about Khadijah (RA) more than people probably expect a twenty-five-year-old to think about a woman who lived fourteen centuries ago. She ran her own trade caravans. She had status, money, and — this part gets skipped — she had already turned down other proposals from powerful, wealthy men before she chose who she chose. She wasn’t waiting anxiously for whoever would have her. She watched how a man handled her business, her workers, her trust, and then she made the first move herself, on her own terms, at an age everyone around her had probably already decided was “getting late.” Her story is told in every khutbah as the ideal. It is rarely told as what it actually was: a woman with standards, acting on them, unbothered by what anyone whispered about her timeline.


I’m not going to pretend the fear isn’t real, because it is, and it’s not stupid. I’ve done the math at 2am — how the pool narrows every year, how someone I know who “settled a little” seems fine, maybe even happy, how there’s a version of me at a wedding in five years being asked, gently and cruelly, if I’m “still being so picky.” That fear is legitimate. It’s just not evidence that what I noticed about a person wasn’t real.


So here’s where I’ve landed, and I’m writing it down because I need to keep reminding myself: there’s a difference between a standard and a fantasy. A fantasy is height, income, a certain look, a certain job title people can brag about at gatherings. Nobody owes you loosening on those. But a standard is — does he speak to his mother the way he’ll one day speak to me. Does his practice of deen make him gentler or does it just make him louder around family. Does he listen when I disagree, or does he wait me out. Those aren’t preferences I can afford to negotiate away just because saying no again is exhausting and everyone in the room wants me to say yes.


Allah says He created spouses for us so that we may find *sakinah* in them — tranquility (30:21). Not tolerance. Not a peace that only holds because you’ve stopped expecting anything that would disturb it. I don’t think you arrive at that by lowering the bar until it’s easy to clear. I think you arrive at it by knowing exactly what peace feels like in your body, and refusing every version of a man who doesn’t give you that, even the ones your whole family has already approved of before he’s proven anything.


I’m still figuring this out in real time. I still hear the same lines. I still, some nights, wonder if I’m the problem. But I needed to put this somewhere I could come back to: my standards were never the obstacle. They were the only thing standing between me and saying yes out of exhaustion, guilt, and a fear of being talked about.


That’s not pickiness. That’s just refusing to forget what I’m worth while everyone else is timing me.
